title: Cache Fundamentals
summary: The small, fast memory that makes the CPU feel fast. Learn cache lines, hits/misses, and how addresses map into a cache.

blocks.markdown:
A **CPU cache** is a small, very fast memory sitting between the CPU and main memory (RAM) that keeps a copy of recently used data.

- RAM is far slower than the CPU — a cache hides that gap.
- It works because programs reuse the same data and nearby data repeatedly.
- Every load/store checks the cache first, RAM only on a miss.
- See [memory-hierarchy](memory-hierarchy) for where it sits overall.

blocks.subTitle: Why caching works
blocks.markdown:
Two habits programs have, called **locality**.

| Locality | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Temporal | Data used once will likely be used again soon |
| Spatial | Nearby data will likely be used soon too |

Caches exploit both — keep what you used, and grab its neighbors.

The cache never moves single bytes — it moves fixed-size chunks called **cache lines** (or blocks), typically 64 bytes.

- A miss pulls in the whole line containing the byte you asked for.
- That's spatial locality in action: neighbors arrive for free.
- The cache is just an array of **line slots**, each holding one line's data plus bookkeeping.

Every access is one of two outcomes.

- **Cache hit** — the data is already in the cache. Fast, done in a cycle or few.
- **Cache miss** — the data isn't there. The CPU stalls while the line is fetched from a slower level (or RAM).
- **Hit rate** — fraction of accesses that hit. Even 90% still leaves costly misses, so design matters.

To look up an address, the cache splits it into three fields.

- **Offset** — which byte inside the line (line size decides its width).
- **Index** — which cache slot (or set) to check.
- **Tag** — the remaining upper bits, stored alongside the data to confirm *which* line this actually is.

All three together reconstruct the full address.

Bigger index → more slots. Bigger offset → bigger lines.

Given an address, the cache follows one procedure.

1. Use the **index** to jump straight to a slot (or set).
2. Compare the stored **tag** there to the address's tag.
3. Match + valid → **hit**, read the byte at **offset**. No match → **miss**, fetch from below.

Step 2 is why the tag must be kept — the index alone is ambiguous.

blocks.subTitle: Direct-mapped
blocks.markdown:
**Direct-mapped**: every address maps to exactly **one** possible slot, chosen by its index.

- Lookup is simple and fast — one tag to compare.
- Problem: two hot addresses that share an index keep **evicting** each other, even with plenty of free space elsewhere. This is a **conflict miss**.

blocks.subTitle: Fully associative
blocks.markdown:
**Fully associative**: an address can go in **any** slot at all — no index, only a tag.

- No conflict misses — a line only leaves when the whole cache is full.
- Cost: every lookup must compare the tag against **every** slot in parallel, which is expensive in hardware. Only practical for small caches.

blocks.subTitle: Set-associative
blocks.markdown:
**Set-associative**: the middle ground. Slots are grouped into **sets**; the index picks a set, then the tag is compared against just the few slots (the *ways*) inside it.

- A **4-way** set-associative cache has 4 slots per set.
- Fewer conflicts than direct-mapped, cheaper than fully associative — what most real CPU caches use.

All three place a line differently and trade off the same way.

| Scheme | Placement | Conflict misses |
|---|---|---|
| Direct-mapped | 1 fixed slot | Most |
| Set-associative | N slots in a set | Some |
| Fully associative | Any slot | None |

More placement freedom always costs more comparison hardware.

**Associativity** is how many slots an address can choose from (1 for direct-mapped, N for N-way, all for fully associative).

- Higher associativity → fewer conflict misses, better hit rate.
- Higher associativity → more parallel tag comparisons → more power, more silicon, slightly slower per lookup.
- Real designs pick 4-way or 8-way as the sweet spot.

What this looks like on a real CPU:

- **L1 cache** — smallest, fastest, often 8-way set-associative, split into instruction and data caches.
- **L2 / L3** — bigger, slower, still set-associative, shared across cores.
- Line size is almost always **64 bytes** across modern CPUs.

Common mistakes:

- **"Bigger cache always means fewer misses."** Poor associativity or bad access patterns can still cause conflict misses in a large cache.
- **"The cache stores by address."** It stores by tag within a slot chosen by index — the index isn't part of the stored data.
- **"Fully associative is strictly better."** It removes conflict misses but its comparison cost limits it to small caches.

blocks.subTitle: Direct-mapped vs set-associative vs fully associative
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Direct-mapped vs set-associative vs fully associative — how do they differ?**

Direct-mapped gives each address exactly one slot (fast, more conflicts). Fully associative allows any slot (no conflicts, costly parallel compare). Set-associative groups slots into small sets and searches only within one set — the practical middle ground almost every real cache uses.

blocks.subTitle: What is a cache line
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a cache line, and why not cache single bytes?**

A cache line (block) is the fixed-size chunk, commonly 64 bytes, that moves between cache and memory as one unit. Fetching whole lines exploits spatial locality — the neighbors of a requested byte are usually needed soon, so grabbing them now avoids future misses.

blocks.subTitle: How an address maps to a set
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How does a memory address map to a cache set?**

The address splits into tag, index, and offset. The index bits are used directly as a set number, so a fixed set of middle address bits always lands in the same set. The tag stored in that set's slots then disambiguates which specific line is present.

blocks.subTitle: Hit vs miss cost
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why is a cache miss so much costlier than a hit?**

A hit is answered from on-chip SRAM in a few cycles. A miss stalls the CPU while the request travels to a slower level, or all the way to RAM, which can take hundreds of cycles. That gap is exactly why hit rate dominates real-world performance.

blocks.subTitle: What is a tag
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is a tag, and why is it stored per line?**

The tag is the upper bits of an address not used for the index or offset. Since many addresses share the same index, the tag is stored with each line so a lookup can confirm the cached line is really the one requested, not just one that happens to hash to the same slot.

blocks.subTitle: Why associativity has a limit
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why don't all caches just use full associativity?**

Full associativity needs every slot's tag compared in parallel for every access — the comparison hardware grows with cache size, burning power and adding delay. Set-associative caps the comparisons to one set's worth, keeping most of the conflict-miss benefit at a fraction of the cost.
